name: manifest_db
description: List an iOS backup's map: for each file id in Manifest.db its domain, relative path, kind, the metadata of its keyed archive (size, mode, owner, protection class, inode, three times) and the state of the blob the id names (present, missing, a directory, a link never followed, not applicable, or refused). It does not rebuild a file system, open or decrypt a payload, or read a password. It reads the backup's plain files (Manifest.plist, Info.plist, Status.plist) for the encryption flag, the device, the backup's version and date and its completion state (completion: finished, not_finished or unknown, from Status.plist's SnapshotState; a backup that did not finish makes the status partial, and unknown, as when there is no Status.plist, is said and is not a failure). Encryption is three-valued: encrypted, not_encrypted, or unknown (Manifest.plist missing, unreadable or without IsEncrypted: never read as unencrypted). An encrypted backup is never reported as empty: when Manifest.db opens as SQLite its rows are listed with payload_encrypted true; when it does not, the answer says the listing is not available and what the file was. No decryption is provided by this tool or this pack. SENSITIVE: key material in Manifest.plist (the key bag, the manifest key) is reported as present with its length and never printed, hashed or previewed (the device's own identifiers in the plain plists, such as the serial number, UDID, IMEI, MEID, ICCID and phone number, are printed as they are), and a path component shaped like a recovery password is withheld from every path, and contains and domain are applied to the path and the domain as the answer prints them (a withheld component is the placeholder), so no filter can ask whether the withheld text matches; the tool writes no values file. Recovery-password shapes are withheld in the forms a key is saved in, not only the dashed one: 42 or more decimal digits (seven groups of six) with at most three characters that are neither a letter nor a digit between two digits, after NFKC folding (any separator: comma, colon, semicolon, plus, brackets, quote marks, hash, accents, symbols, dashes of any kind, dots, underscores, a zero-width character, a run of white space as one; no separator at all; full-width and Arabic-Indic digits), and a key split across two path components is withheld in each (the slash is such a character); a name with fewer digits is printed. A path or a domain longer than 8,192 characters is not judged and is printed as <name too long to judge withheld> (nothing a file system holds is that long; judging it would cost the cell's length: the pattern before this cost 0.46 s per MB of 41 digits and a letter, repeated, outside max_seconds, and now judging is linear and a path costs at most 8,192 characters). Every statement SQLite runs is ended at max_seconds and by a stop signal, not only the rows: a table b-tree whose pages point at each other (a Manifest.db of 10 KB) kept the count of the rows going for ever, and a stop signal waited for it. The count of the Files table (files_in_manifest) is given a tenth of max_seconds, and an answer without it says so (null). The domains are listed by the text printed, so a withheld domain does not stand where its hidden name sorts. file_id is the SHA-1 of the domain and the real path and is printed for a withheld path too: it is the blob's name in the backup directory, and the listing of that directory shows the same digest, so printing it adds no oracle (it cannot be inverted for a 48-digit key, and confirms a guess at a short name, as the directory does). Times are NOT guessed: epoch (unix by default, or apple) is applied to every time, the raw seconds are returned beside the ISO 8601 UTC time, and the earliest and latest non-zero value read are in the answer (a zero is converted and returned, and left out of the range); epoch.consistency counts, per field, the times that fall after the backup's own date or before 2007 under the epoch applied. The wrong epoch is a 31-year shift (Apple against Unix), not a range of decades: check the epoch against a file whose time the case documents. Metadata comes from the keyed archive's root ($top.root, followed through UID references with a depth bound and a cycle check), not from the first object with a Size. A file id is validated (40 hexadecimal digits) before it is joined to a path, and the path must stay inside the backup; both the sharded layout (<xx>/<id>) and the flat one are looked for. A -wal or -journal beside Manifest.db is copied with it to a working directory under $OUT and opened there, never the original; a Manifest.db that is a symbolic link is refused, and a -wal or -journal that is one is not followed or copied (it is said). A Manifest.db that is not SQLite is described by its size and, if it has 256 bytes or more, the entropy of its first 4 KiB, never its first bytes; a TEXT cell that is not UTF-8 does not stop the listing (its bytes show as escapes); the keyed archive of a row is read only when the cell is a BLOB of at most 1 MiB (a larger cell is not read: metadata_status too_large, with its size), a cell that is not a BLOB is said without being read, and rows with no readable metadata are counted in an observation and make the status partial; the plain plists (Manifest.plist, Info.plist, Status.plist) are read when they are at most 4 MiB (a larger one is said: status too_large, and the answer is partial); when Status.plist is missing the basis of a complete answer says the completion is unknown, not that the backup finished; the name columns (fileID, domain, relativePath) are read to their first 8,193 characters, one more than is judged, so a cell of tens of megabytes is never made into a string of that size in Python (SQLite itself holds the cell once while it cuts it, so memory follows the largest TEXT cell once); the Files table is read in row order, never through the file-id index, so a damaged index page does not cost the listing; a damaged page ends the listing with read_error and what was read is kept (status partial); a Manifest.db cut inside its last page is said and is partial, and one with fewer pages than its header declares does not open and is refused, never listed as empty. The answer is strict JSON: a number that is not finite is {"_float": text}. The whole listing is kept: the inline page is limit rows and the rest is in the file the answer names. status is complete, or partial (the listing is not available, the time limit stopped it (an observation says after how many rows), a page is damaged or the file is cut short, contains ran out of time on a path, a companion that is a link was not applied, the metadata of a listed row is not in the answer, whatever the reason (metadata_status too_large, malformed, not_keyed_archive or absent: a cell over the size limit, one that is not a blob, a blob that is not a keyed archive, a NULL cell), or the backup did not finish).

path.description: The backup directory, or its Manifest.db

contains.description: Case-insensitive regex over the relative path as the answer prints it (a path component shaped like a recovery password is the placeholder there; at most 1000 characters); a path on which it runs longer than 2 seconds (or past max_seconds) is counted and not matched, and the answer says partial

domain.description: Only this domain exactly, as the answer prints it, e.g. HomeDomain or AppDomain-com.example

epoch.description: unix (default) or apple: the epoch the file times are counted from. Never inferred; check it against a file whose time the case documents

limit.description: Entries (and domains) in the inline answer (default 200, and at most 1 MiB of rows); the whole list is in the file the answer names

max_seconds.description: Stop reading rows after this long (default 240, at most 255); the answer says partial and where it stopped. The clock is read on every row, contains included, and inside every statement SQLite runs (the count of the table gets a tenth of it)
